analysis.one_liner: Eliminates the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the agency that polices credit cards, mortgages, and loans.
analysis.headline: The Repeal CFPB Act, which would abolish the federal consumer financial watchdog, died in the Senate Banking Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the 2010 law that created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the agency that writes and enforces rules for credit cards, mortgages, payday loans, debt collection, and credit reporting. Wiping the law off the books would eliminate the agency and restore the older legal framework as if the 2010 reforms had never happened. The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, banks, credit card issuers, mortgage lenders, debt collectors, and credit reporting agencies would be free of the CFPB's rulemaking, supervision, and enforcement — the watchdog that can order refunds and penalties when these companies treat consumers unfairly. Consumers would lose that federal referee.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the Consumer Financial Protection Act of 2010 outright and revives prior law as if it had never been passed, eliminating the CFPB and its authority over banks, lenders, debt collectors, and credit reporting agencies.
Financial companies regulated by the CFPB would be freed from its rulemaking, supervision, and enforcement actions over consumer credit products.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary consumers, who would lose the federal agency charged with protecting them from unfair or deceptive practices in credit cards, mortgages, debt collection, and credit reports.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the statute would revive the prior legal framework as if the 2010 Act had never been enacted, unwinding not just the Bureau but the post-2008 consumer-protection structure it carries.

Critics of the CFPB argue it is an unaccountable agency with a single director and its own funding stream; this bill responds by eliminating the consumer watchdog entirely rather than restructuring it, leaving no federal agency with consumer financial protection as its core mission.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit runs entirely to financial firms freed from the CFPB's rulemaking and enforcement; its cost falls on ordinary consumers, who would lose the single federal agency whose job is policing credit cards, mortgages, debt collection, and payday loans for unfair or deceptive practices. The repeal also revives prior law as if the 2010 Act never existed, undoing the post-2008 consumer-protection framework wholesale rather than targeting specific rules.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote, dying when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Ted Cruz introduced the bill on April 13, 2021, with five Republican cosponsors.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee.
No further action was ever taken; the bill died in committee when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary consumers keep the CFPB and its protections; banks and lenders remain subject to its oversight.

for.what_they_did: Held the bill in committee without a hearing, markup, or vote; no action was taken after referral.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had six Republican sponsors and cosponsors and no Democratic or Independent support, and it died in a committee controlled by Democrats without any vote.

industries.industry: Banks, consumer lenders, debt collectors, and credit reporting agencies

Consumers would lose the federal agency charged with policing credit cards, mortgages, debt collection, and credit reports.

industries.industry: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (its own staff and operations)
industries.note: The bill would eliminate the agency itself, ending its functions and returning the relevant legal framework to pre-2010 law.
